derives_from: Two things, and the first is the unusual one. **The phonology is taken verbatim from this repository's own Hindi table, `hi__hi-IN.json`, because Hindi and Urdu are one spoken language.** Every question a respelling table asks -- which vowel an Urdu reader hears English /æ/ as, whether /v/ and /w/ are one phoneme, what to do with a tone letter, which onsets the reader can begin a word with -- has the same answer for both, so re-deriving them would have been re-deriving Hindi's work with a chance of getting it differently rather than better. `reader_onsets` below is Hindi's list unchanged, for exactly that reason: it is a claim about the reader's phonotactics and the reader is the same. What changes is the orthography, and that is the second source: **the transcription convention Urdu print already uses for foreign words**, which is not codified anywhere but is uniform, and is attested inside this corpus by the Urdu pack's own loanwords -- ٹکٹ, ڈاکٹر, اسٹیشن, کارڈ, ٹیکسی, پاسپورٹ, ایمبولینس, وائی فائی, تھیٹر, ہاؤس. The vocalised register is the one this column is written in, because that is what an Urdu dictionary and a school primer use and it is the only register in which a foreign word can be read aloud without guessing; an Urdu newspaper writes the same words unpointed. There is no national standard to borrow: the Muqtadira Qaumi Zaban's technical dictionaries transcribe English terms this way but publish no table, and BGN/PCGN 2007 runs in the other direction -- Urdu into Latin -- which is what `romanization_bgn` in the pack uses and is not this.

deviations.rule: t d -> ٹ ڈ, and t̪ d̪ -> ت د
deviations.why: The Hindi table maps both series to the dental त/द. Urdu's own loanword orthography contradicts that in every instance: ٹکٹ, ڈاکٹر, اسٹیشن, کارڈ, ٹیکسی, پاسپورٹ, ہوٹل, ٹرین, بیٹری, and the place names اٹلی, پولینڈ, کینیڈا, سویڈن, اسکاٹ لینڈ. Urdu's ت and د are dental; an English or European alveolar is perceptually nearer the retroflex, and that is the letter Urdu reaches for. The corpus's `ipa` column marks the genuinely dental stops with U+032A, so this table can keep the two apart where the Hindi one merges them -- the one place this table is more accurate than the table it derives from.

Both the Arabic and the Persian tables spell /θ/ with ث. Urdu owns ث and pronounces it /s/, so it would give a reader the wrong sound. Urdu has an aspirate series instead and its own print uses it -- تھینک یو, تھیٹر, تھری -- so /θ/ is written with a letter pair that actually says [tʰ], which is the substitution an Urdu speaker makes. This is the open question the Persian table's own report ends on, answered the other way because Urdu has a letter Persian does not.

The voiced partner is *not* symmetrical with /θ/. دھ is a breathy-voiced dental stop, and breathiness is the wrong feature to add to a fricative; Urdu print writes /ð/ as a plain dental stop -- دی for *the*, فادر for *Father*. ذ is refused for the same reason ث is: Urdu pronounces it /z/.

deviations.rule: ق خ غ are kept as distinct letters
deviations.why: The Hindi table has to merge /q/ into क, /x/ into ख and /ɣ/ into ग, because Devanagari's nukta forms are not part of ordinary Hindi print. Urdu owns all three letters and uses them every day (قیمت, خدا, غلط), so three distinctions the sister table loses survive here. The same holds for ژ, which is in the Urdu alphabet and is the only letter for /ʒ/ -- without it French *je* and *zéro* would spell alike.

Arabic's reason, re-checked for Urdu: the script is cursive and a hyphen breaks the join, so a separator would print a visibly broken word. Hebrew takes the hyphen because it has no joining forms, which is the test -- and Urdu is on Arabic's side of it, as Persian is.

Every device the engine carries is unavailable. `caps` is a no-op on a caseless script; `acute` and `grave` need an entry in `VOWEL_LETTERS`, which lists no Perso-Arabic letter, and both slots around the letter are already occupied by the harakat this notation writes; and `prime` is out for Arabic's and Persian's reason -- U+02B9 is a Latin-block modifier letter and reorders inside a right-to-left run. Saying so is better than configuring a device that does nothing, which is what `content/CONTRIBUTING.md` asks for.

deviations.rule: the harakat are written, and the sukun is not
deviations.why: The Arabic and Persian tables write a sukun on every vowelless consonant. Urdu's own dictionary practice marks the vowels and leaves the absences bare -- Feroz-ul-Lughat and a school primer both do -- so this table follows it. It halves the number of marks on a card set at 4.4-5.4pt, where the Hebrew note records 0.20pt as the smallest ink this paper holds, and it costs nothing: an unmarked Urdu consonant is already read with no vowel.

deviations.rule: geminates are a doubled letter, not a tashdid
deviations.why: Both are Urdu. The doubled letter is chosen on the same size argument: a tashdid would stack a second mark on a letter that usually already carries a harakat, and the card has width to spare where it has no vertical room.

Not a choice -- Urdu orthography has no medial noon ghunna. Every nasal vowel therefore carries two rules: ں where the syllable ends the word, and ن everywhere else, which is the same sound and the letter Urdu actually writes there (انگریزی, بند).

deviations.rule: ے is written only word-finally, and ی carries /eː/ and /iː/ apart by the mark before it
deviations.why: Also orthography rather than choice. What makes it work is Urdu's three-way vocalisation of ی and و: bare ی is /eː/, zer + ی is /iː/, zabar + ی is /ɛː/, and the same three for و give /oː/, /uː/ and /ɔː/. That is six vowel qualities plus length, where the Arabic table's own note records a three-quality ceiling and Persian's records six -- so this is the widest vowel system any right-to-left reader here has.

deviations.rule: ʔ and ʕ are dropped rather than written with ع
deviations.why: ع is silent in Urdu. Writing it would put a letter on the page that an Urdu reader pronounces as nothing, which is the same objection that removes BGN's ‘ from `romanization_bgn` in the pack.

approximations.why: Urdu has no letter for English LOT or THOUGHT and merges them with /aː/, which is what its print does: ڈاکٹر, کالج, آفس, اسٹاپ, شاپ. The Hindi table can keep them apart with ऑ, a letter Devanagari added for English; Perso-Arabic never did. So *not* and *nought* spell alike.
One Urdu phoneme, one letter. *Vine* and *wine* spell alike, which is also how an Urdu speaker says them.
Urdu has no front rounded vowel. German ü and French u become /juː/, and ö and eu become /oː/ -- the substitutions an Urdu speaker makes, and the ones the Hindi table makes with यू and ओ.
Approximations even after the deviation above: [tʰ] is a stop and [θ] is a fricative. They are the nearest sounds Urdu has and the ones its own print uses.
Urdu's ح and ہ are both /h/, so a separate letter for the pharyngeal would be spelling and not sound.

Klingon's lateral fricative. Urdu has no lateral fricative at all and no letter that suggests one; ل is what the Hindi table does with it too. The affricate /t͡ɬ/ is written تل, two letters, because that is at least the right place of articulation twice.
Mandarin, Thai and Vietnamese tone is dropped. Urdu has no tone and no mark for one, and the vertical slots a tone mark could use are taken by the harakat.

legend: زیر زبر پیش لکھے ہیں، کیونکہ وہی تلفظ ہیں۔ کوئی نیا حرف نہیں۔
note: Reader's legend, per content/RESPELL-SYSTEMS.md's one-line rule. Urdu's is the ko/sw shape rather than the ar shape: there is no new letter to teach, because every letter this notation uses is in the ordinary Urdu alphabet -- including ژ ق خ غ, which are everyday letters here and not the extended set the Arabic table has to argue about. What the legend has to say instead is why the marks are there, since an Urdu reader meets an unpointed spelling in a newspaper and a pointed one in a dictionary, and this column is the dictionary register.
